Field observations of captive colonies indicate that the initial wet weight of a freshly laid egg is 5.68 grams [Ww0 = 5.68 grams], a value that accounts for both the embryonic tissues and the substantial albumen and yolk reserves required to sustain development through the incubation period. This relatively high egg-to-female mass ratio aligns with the general pattern observed in altricial psittaciforms, which allocate significant resources to each offspring prior to hatching.

A pronounced sexual size dimorphism emerges as nestlings transition through the fledgling stage and into adulthood. This modest dimorphism is consistent with the subtle differences in body size observed across most cockatoo species, where males typically outweigh females by a small margin, and is likely linked to the species' monogamous mating system, which places comparable metabolic demands on both sexes during the breeding season.

In birds maintained at a steady ambient temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], which corresponds to the upper boundary of their thermoneutral zone, sexual maturity is attained at 94.5 days after hatching [tp = 94.5 days after hatching]. This relatively early onset of gonadal activation is notable among cockatoos, as most related species require longer developmental periods before reaching puberty. The accelerated maturation may represent an adaptation to the unpredictable rainfall patterns of the Australian interior, where ephemeral resource pulses favor rapid life cycles that allow individuals to capitalize on short-lived breeding opportunities. Year-round captive colonies confirm that this timing is consistent across generations when thermal conditions are held constant.

First breeding in this species is typically deferred until well after puberty, reflecting the additional time required to secure a nest cavity and establish a durable pair bond. The time since birth at first brood is 456 days [tR = 456 days] when birds are housed at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], a delay that allows subadults to refine foraging skills and accumulate sufficient body condition for the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The strategic postponement of first reproduction likely enhances lifetime fitness by reducing the risk of nest failure associated with inexperienced parenting, a common selective pressure among long-lived avian taxa with extended parental care periods.
